items.title: Hollow lit cones are laterally off-axis from their dark cones, so the emissive collapses at yaw 315. cone() rotates each primitive about its own origin, so two cones sharing rot=(11,-8,0) but sitting at different z have parallel axes offset by ~0.045 world units (~4px): the lit cone pokes out on the +x+y side and hides behind the dark cone from the opposite camera. Measured glow coverage hollow_shard 0.0061 at y315 vs 0.024-0.036 elsewhere; hollow_echo 0.0089 vs 0.042-0.068. Currently latent because anchor_view.gd only ever draws y045 (see the sibling item). Fix is to put the lit cone on the dark cone's rotated axis, or to build both from one origin, and it applies to the whole Hollow set at once rather than shard alone

Board camera: pan and zoom. Pan on middle-drag plus lf_* keys and edge-scroll, NOT left-drag — left click arms builds and selects emplacements, so drag-to-pan turns every slipped click into a camera move. The board cursor should carry the camera with it, which gives keyboard and gamepad panning without a second system. anchor_sim._step's splash loop tests 'u == target' but Godot 4.7 compares Dictionary by value (probed: two dicts with equal contents are ==, and Array.find matches by value), while sim/engine.py tests 'u is target'. Two units of the same kind with equal hp and equal dist therefore drop out of splash damage in GDScript and take it in Python. Latent only because same-kind units spawn on different ticks so their dist differs — a wave table that spawns two identical units on the same tick turns it into a parity failure. Found while deciding where facing state could live (LF-050); the fix is an identity-safe test on the GDScript side, e.g. comparing by index
items.note: fixed by comparing target by index; Godot Dictionary == is a value comparison, probed

The gate's rendered checks read display state from the player's save. window_mode, resolution and ui_scale live in user://progress.json, which is outside the repo, so game renders / menu renders / accessibility measured whatever the last person left set — the same tree reported coverage 0.56 and 0.34 on two machines, and the a11y analyser samples its background colours out of those frames. The game renders gate check took 2,187,910 ms (36 min) on one run and then PASSED, against 2,493 ms on another run of the same tree the same day. CAUSE, observed by the owner: the three rendered checks launch a REAL Godot window (GL Compatibility reads back nothing headlessly), and macOS throttles a window it considers occluded — cover it, background it, or just keep working in front of it and the frame loop stalls, so main.gd's 'await RenderingServer.frame_post_draw' never resolves. The run does not fail, it waits until the window is visible again and then passes, which is why the gate stayed green. Two mitigations are in: tools/check.py bounds every subprocess (DEFAULT_TIMEOUT 300s, PARITY_TIMEOUT 1800s) and reaps grandchildren on timeout, so a stall is now a red run naming the check; and --no-window skips the three windowed checks so the gate is usable while someone is at the machine. Neither is a fix. A real fix makes the capture independent of the compositor presenting frames — candidates: RenderingServer.force_draw() instead of awaiting frame_post_draw, or rendering the shot through a SubViewport. Both need probing against Godot 4.7.1 on this machine, and the occlusion stall has to be reproduced on purpose first (cover the window during a --shot run) or there is no way to tell a fix from a coincidence

(1) Built-in agents — Explore, Plan, general-purpose — have no .claude/agents/*.md frontmatter to carry model: sonnet, so they inherit the parent (Opus) unless the model is passed at each call site. mask_glow.py re-saves every glow PNG in the manifest on every run, not only the ones a render actually changed. PIL's save() does not reproduce identical bytes for identical pixel content across invocations, so re-running it after a partial re-render (e.g. --only one asset) touches every other sprite's LFS blob with a pixel-identical but byte-different file — confirmed via git-lfs smudge + numpy compare on hollow_column_y045_glow.png: max abs pixel diff 0, but sha256 differs from HEAD. Harmless to the game, but it turns every glow-pass re-render into a full-repo LFS diff and makes 'what actually changed' unreadable from git status. Fix: skip re-saving a glow PNG whose computed output already matches what is on disk, or track per-file content hashes the way pack_atlas.py already does for the atlas page.

The --autoplay smoke policy (_autobuild_step in anchor_view.gd) fills every free slot with the single highest-priority-affordable tower in Content.unlocked_at() order, so a board never shows a mix of weapon classes -- confirmed while trying to screenshot a mortar/flak burst for the combat-FX pass: anchor-09, anchor-13, anchor-16 and anchor-21 all built out one tower type (arc-node or anchor-damper) and never touched flak-array or mortar-emplacement even many waves in. This is the same root cause LF-053 already names for grading. A '--build <tower-id> <slot-x>,<slot-y>' CLI hook in main.gd would let --shot verify a specific weapon's FX/behaviour on demand without fighting the autobuild policy.

tools/shot.py's --extra nargs='*' cannot pass any flag-shaped token (--scroll 3, --paused, --select 1) -- argparse classifies any argv item starting with '-' as option-like and refuses to fold it into nargs='*', so 'unrecognized arguments' aborts before Godot ever launches. Confirmed with a standalone argparse repro, not anchor-specific. The tool's own docstring/epilog example ('--extra --select 1 --pick pulse-turret') has apparently never actually been run. Workaround used this session: invoke the native Linux Godot binary directly under xvfb-run with the same argv tools/toolpaths.godot_argv() builds, bypassing shot.py's argparse. Fix is probably nargs=argparse.REMAINDER (consumes everything after --extra verbatim, order-preserved) rather than nargs='*'.

scripts/anchor_view.gd's boot() hands sim.setup() Content.towers/Content.enemies/Content.anchor(anchor_id) directly -- scripts/loadout.gd (Loadout.towers()/enemies()/anchor()) is never called anywhere in the codebase. Confirmed by grep. Six of the nine recovery effects (tower_draw_mult, bounty_mult, starting_funds_add, tower_damage_mult, range_mult, and by extension anything Loadout would apply) are therefore completely inert regardless of what the player owns -- only the three effects read directly at their call sites (sell_refund_add, surge_charge_mult, veterancy_mult) do anything, and this session wired those three in (Threshold Surge charge rate, veterancy rank thresholds). Fix is almost certainly three lines in anchor_view.gd's boot(): sim.setup(Loadout.anchor(anchor), Loadout.towers(Content.towers), Loadout.enemies(Content.enemies), difficulty). Left unfixed this session because it is a between-anchor progression system gap discovered while wiring the abilities/pacing/targeting/veterancy task, not part of that task, and scripts/loadout.gd is out of scope to touch.

Rebuilding .godot/ blanks the level for anyone playing out of the same tree. The owner plays from D:\dev\Latticefall while agents edit /mnt/d/dev/Latticefall — the same directory. An agent moved .godot aside to force a cold import and the running game lost every imported texture: menu still drew (plain UI), level came up blank. Diagnosed as a code regression for a full pass before the real cause surfaced. Also: an import performed by the Linux Godot build is not sufficient for the Windows editor, which re-imports on open — that was the step that actually restored it. Mitigation is documented in CLAUDE.md; a mechanical version would be a guard in tools/ that refuses to touch .godot while a Godot process is live, or a shot.py flag that imports in place rather than cold

THEATRE SCALE 01. Board camera: pan, zoom, edge-scroll and cursor-follow. At 48x48 and above the board exceeds the viewport several times over, so this stops being a convenience and becomes how the game is read. Scoping is in docs/STATE.md under LF-052, with two corrections from this session: AnchorView.position is now taken by the screen-shake trauma system so a camera must compose with it rather than own the transform, and Backdrop sizes itself to the raw viewport independently of the board so scaling the parent would tear it
items.why: Nothing larger than one screen is playable without it
items.note: Landed: CAM-01. ZOOM_MIN is derived per-board from tile extent vs. the strip (decision 056), floored at 0.05 so the projection cannot degenerate. Verified on anchor-24 (2112px board) at 100% and 200% interface scale.

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 02. Cull and cache board tile drawing. _draw_board() is O(w*h) every frame with no culling and no caching; at 64x64 that is 4096 tile draws per frame before a single unit moves. Needs viewport culling plus a cached static layer, since ground, path and slot tiles never change during a level
items.why: First thing that falls over as the board grows

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 03. Spatial hash for target acquisition. _step() is O(emplacements x units) with an inner O(units) splash loop; at 60 emplacements and 400 units that is 24000 distance checks per tick at 30 Hz. Needs grid bucketing or per-tower target caching with a re-acquire interval. Must be mirrored in sim/engine.py and must not change WHICH unit is selected, or parity breaks
items.why: Sim cost is the hard ceiling on unit count
items.note: Closed by WAR-03 (#67). The item described _step() as O(emplacements x units) with an inner O(units) splash loop — 24000 distance checks per tick at 60 emplacements and 400 units at 30 Hz — and required that the fix be mirrored in sim/engine.py and not change WHICH unit is selected. Both conditions met. Measured: 512 units/60 towers/24 segments went 20.08 ms -> 0.84 ms per tick (24.1x), and 1000/80/32 went 58.43 ms -> 1.73 ms (33.8x). Selection was verified directly rather than inferred, with 0 differing selections across four independent modes including an LF-055-shaped identical-units-same-tick case and every anchor x difficulty x policy driven through the real Sim.run(). Decision 072 records the ordering contract that makes it safe.

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 04. Minimap with threat and power overlay. Once the board exceeds the screen the player cannot see where the trouble is; the minimap becomes the primary readout for lane pressure and for which region of the grid is browned out
items.why: The player cannot defend what they cannot see

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 05. Large-board authoring tooling. Hand-authoring a 64x64 multi-lane anchor is not viable and the generator has to exist before the content does. Extends tools/densify.py's preview-first method: generate layout plus lane set plus slot placement, preview it, then grade it
items.why: The generator must precede the content

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 06. Multi-lane paths and multiple spawn points. The structural blocker: anchor JSON carries a single path array, and anchor_sim.gd and sim/engine.py are both built around one point_at(), one path_length and a leak test of dist >= path_length. Supporting 2-5 simultaneous lanes and up to 4 spawn points is what makes a front line exist at all. Both rule implementations must move together or parity is lost
items.why: Without it there is no flank, only a longer queue

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 07. Raise the unit budget to 250-400 alive. Depends on the spatial hash. Also needs the drawables() rebuild reviewed: it allocates and sorts an Array of Dictionaries and is called several times per frame across the view, the glow layer and both FX layers
items.why: Mass is what makes ground feel contested rather than queued

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 08. Unit roles and formations: screens, breakers, siege. Four hundred units walking single file is not an army. Needs units that advance together, shield each other, and behave differently when the lane ahead is blocked
items.why: Behaviour is what turns a crowd into an attack

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 09. Relay nodes: player-built power generation placed on the board, feeding a radius around themselves. Turns capacity from a number handed down by the brief into ground the player takes and defends. Rule change, so it must be mirrored in sim/engine.py
items.why: Makes supply something you hold rather than something you are given

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 10. The pulse: an enemy attack that suppresses rather than damages, taking every emplacement inside a radius offline for a few seconds. The counter is depth and redundancy rather than more damage. Note _covered_by() is a radius test over placed emplacements with no notion of a timed effect ON an emplacement, so this needs a new effect shape in both rule implementations
items.why: The enemy needs an answer to a dense line that is not just more hit points

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 11. Per-node power grid, so supply is regional rather than one global capacity_mw. Losing a flank should cost the guns on that flank. Large rules change; check first whether it can be expressed as data plus an existing effect type before adding a new rule shape
items.why: One global number cannot survive a board this size

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 12. Siege Battery: multi-tube salvo with a long reload, arcing over the whole board, drawing almost nothing between salvos and enormously during one. The first weapon that spikes the bus rather than loading it, which is a genuinely new shape for the power economy
items.why: A new shape of draw, not just a bigger number

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 13. Cutting Lance: a sustained beam held on one target with damage ramping the longer it holds, so switching targets wastes it. Needs a persistent-beam FX class; the current beam class is a 0.18s snap, not a held state
items.why: A gun that punishes target switching

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 14. Spine Driver: charges off spare bus capacity and fires a line that pierces everything in it. The only weapon that rewards staying UNDER capacity, which inverts the usual pressure and is the reason it is worth building
items.why: Inverts the power pressure the whole game is built on

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 15. Raise the sprite atlas from 256px to 512px cells and add pages. Four times the pixels per cell; orthographic scale is derived from cell width so the projection stays exact. Measure atlas memory and full-library render time on this machine before committing, since the library will also be growing
items.why: Fidelity, and the pipeline is scripted so it is machine time not artist time

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 16. Turret animation: traverse, recoil and reload frames. A turret that visibly turns and recoils sells mass better than any particle effect. Frames are cheap in the atlas and the pivot is already measured, but this multiplies cell count so it interacts with the atlas page budget
items.why: Sells weight better than particles do

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 17. Three environment sets with weather and a hazard each, one per act. Each act already owns an antagonist, a power tier and a mechanic; giving it a place with its own light and ground hazard is what makes the campaign feel like it travels
items.why: Each act should be somewhere, not just a palette

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 18. Dynamic score and battlefield mix responding to wave intensity, so pressure is audible before it is visible. The audio director already ducks music on brownout; this extends that idea to the whole fight
items.why: Intensity should be heard before it is read

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 19. A grading policy that can press a button. THE LARGEST HOLE IN THE PROJECT. sim/engine.py never uses speed, call-wave, the kill chain, an ability, targeting priority or veterancy, so every one of the 24 anchor grades describes a player who uses none of them. That was an acceptable floor when sell() was the only unmodelled verb; it is not acceptable now that a third of the game is unmodelled, and scaling the board multiplies the gap rather than closing it
items.why: Every balance number currently describes a player who never presses anything

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 20. Capped-core policies so a graded build can be mixed. Every Policy is a total preference order and _try_build fills every free slot greedily from the top, so a graded build is all-of-one-thing and claims like this escort makes the cheap gun matter are untestable. Prerequisite for grading a 60-emplacement board meaningfully. Supersedes LF-053
items.why: A 60-slot board graded as all-of-one-thing tells you nothing

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 21. Re-grade the whole campaign at theatre scale. Density targets, leak budgets and the capacity ladder all move with board size, lane count and unit budget; the wave-density gate check will need its act comparison rebased
items.why: Every balance figure moves when the board does

items.title: THEATRE SCALE 22. Performance budget in the gate. A frame-time regression should be a red run rather than a feeling. Needs a fixed-fps timing harness with a per-anchor budget so scaling work cannot silently cost 20ms a frame
items.why: Otherwise performance regresses invisibly

items.title: An emplacement with nothing in range re-scans every unit on every tick, forever. anchor_sim.gd _step(): when target.is_empty() it does p.erase(aim); continue WITHOUT resetting cooldown, which has already gone <= 0 — so the next tick scans all U units again. Same in sim/engine.py. MEASURED: a board whose guns cover a currently empty lane costs 2.19x at 8 towers/32 units rising to 2.87x at 100/800 versus the same board with targets in range. This is exactly the shape a big multi-lane board produces, since most guns are idle most of the time. Fix must be mirrored in both engines and must not change WHICH unit is selected
items.why: 2.9x sim cost for guns that are doing nothing
items.note: Closed incidentally by WAR-03's spatial index (#67). The item measured that an emplacement with nothing in range re-scans every unit every tick forever, costing 2.19x at 8 towers/32 units rising to 2.87x at 100/800 versus the same board with targets in range. With the index, an idle gun scans its OWN EMPTY CELLS rather than the whole board: --all-idle now measures 0.74x — faster than the baseline it used to be nearly three times slower than. No separate fix was needed and none was written; the general solution subsumed the special case. Note decision 058 already recorded that an earlier targeted attempt at this exact problem passed 864-run parity and changed nothing measurable, which is why the number above is a measurement and not an argument.

items.title: _covered_by() is called per unit per tick from the movement loop and iterates EVERY placed emplacement, testing eff.get(type) != effect inside the loop — so it costs O(towers) per unit even when no emplacement on the board has that effect at all. MEASURED: this is the unconditional 0.248-0.275 microseconds per tower-unit pair floor that persists even when only ~4 percent of towers are off cooldown. At 60 towers and 400 units that is 24000 wasted iterations per tick, 30 times a second. Fix is to filter placed by effect type once per tick; about ten lines in each rule file, mirrored
items.why: Pure waste in the hottest loop, paid even when the effect is unused

items.title: fx_additive _draw_hit_flashes() is quadratic in unit count: it scans the live hit list for every unit, and the hit list grows with the number of units being shot. MEASURED at 32x32: 0.31ms at 150 units, 0.96 at 300, 3.67 at 600, 7.67 at 900 — roughly U^1.9, and 29 percent of all draw cost at 900 units. Fix is to key hits by tile bucket rather than scanning. Presentation only, no parity exposure
items.why: The only quadratic term in the renderer

items.title: drawables() is rebuilt and re-sorted FOUR times per frame — anchor_view.gd:1152 and :1154 (shadow and sprite passes), glow_layer.gd:36, fx_additive.gd:209. Each call allocates an Array of one Dictionary per emplacement and per unit, computes depth, yaw and screen position, then sort_custom with a GDScript lambda. MEASURED at about 3.2 microseconds per entity per call, so 12.8 per entity per frame. Building it once and sharing it is 1.46x on its own and 2.47x combined with tile-list caching at 64x64 with 60 emplacements and 400 units. Presentation only
items.why: Four identical rebuilds and sorts per frame

items.title: tools/blender/render.py calibrate() cannot converge at 384 or 1024 px cells. It corrects ORTHO_SCALE from the WIDTH ratio only, so a one pixel height shortfall never resolves — reproduced deterministically: tile 192x95 against expected 192x96, and 512x255 against 512x256. 256 and 512 happen to work by luck. This blocks raising the render base, so it is a prerequisite for any atlas resolution increase. Also note pack_atlas.py has its own hardcoded CELL = 256 that is not read from the manifest, so two constants must move in lockstep
items.why: Blocks raising sprite fidelity at all

items.title: validate_data.py computes board saturation from base draw_mw only and never looks at upgrade.draw_mw, so an emplacement's upgraded draw is invisible to the saturation guard. Latent today; it starts to matter as soon as there are spectacle weapons with steep upgrade draws, which is exactly what the theatre-scale plan adds
items.why: The guard that protects the power decision does not see upgraded draw

items.title: THEATRE SCALE. Sprite legibility at zoom-out is a design problem, not a camera feature. MEASURED: fitting a 64x64 board needs zoom 0.234x at 100 percent interface scale and 0.117x at 200 percent, which renders a 256px sprite at 30-60px on screen — likely below the threshold for telling one enemy type from another. So a big board plus a fixed 256px atlas is a legibility wall. Options are bigger tiles (raising Iso.TILE_W/TILE_H, a whole-game layout change touching every screen-space calculation, the measured pivot and the a11y baselines), a zoom floor with a minimap doing the wide read, or silhouette-first art authored to survive 30px. This needs a human decision before the camera work is finished
items.why: The camera cannot fix what the art cannot show

items.title: PARITY BLIND SPOT: the gate never tests the build the owner plays. tools/test_parity.py goes through toolpaths.godot_argv(), and toolpaths.godot() prefers the native Linux build, so all 864 parity runs compare CPython against LINUX Godot. The owner plays the WINDOWS build. MEASURED across 100000 float64 samples on three runtimes: sqrt, fmod, +-*/, floor, round and manual hypot are byte-identical on all three, but Windows Godot (MSVC UCRT) diverges from CPython and Linux Godot (glibc) on atan2 0.084 percent, sin 0.133, cos 0.120, pow 0.130, log 0.031, exp 0.069 and tan 4.32 percent of samples. The rules currently use none of those ops so parity holds today BY ACCIDENT, not by design. Two fixes, both cheap: run test_parity.py against the Windows build at least once per release, and add a gate check that greps anchor_sim.gd and engine.py for the unsafe op set
items.why: The build that ships is never compared against the reference

items.title: DECISION 030 IS PARTLY WRONG AND IT IS BLOCKING WORK. It says square roots are unsafe in the rules. MEASURED: IEEE-754 requires sqrt to be correctly rounded, both runtimes issue SQRTSD, and sqrt matched 100000 of 100000 samples across CPython, Linux Godot and Windows Godot. The actual culprit in decision 030 was Vector2.distance_to, a FLOAT32 helper: for 2 million points placed exactly on an integer radius, float32 and float64 disagree on the <= r test 10.2 percent of the time. So the rule to carry forward is float64 and never Vector2, NOT never sqrt. This matters because it unblocks off-grid geometry: continuous positions with sqrt-normalised directions ran 4000 ticks x 64 units bit-identical on all three runtimes. Supersede decision 030 with an entry that names the safe op set (+ - * / sqrt fmod floor min max comparisons) and the banned set (atan2 sin cos tan pow log exp, and anything through Vector2)
items.why: A wrong rule is blocking a feature it was never about

items.title: Free placement removes the denominator from the board saturation invariant. validate_data.py bounds capacity_mw against len(slots) x max_draw, and CLAUDE.md plus STATE.md both record this as a trap that already bit once: anchor-24 reached 103 percent of what would run every slot at maximum draw and the power decision the whole game is about had stopped existing on five levels. With no slots, board saturation is unbounded and the check has nothing to divide by. It must be re-derived from something else before free placement ships: a hard emplacement cap, buildable area divided by footprint area, or funds. This is the single biggest non-obvious cost of free placement and it attacks the core hook directly
items.why: Free placement silently deletes the guard protecting the power economy

items.title: YAW_HYSTERESIS_DEG is 12.0 in iso.gd, which is LARGER than half a bucket at 16 yaws (11.25 degrees). If the yaw count is raised to 16 without changing it, an emplacement facing locks permanently and never re-buckets. Decision 049 measured that band empirically at 4 yaws (116 changes with 40 reversals became 59 changes with 3 reversals); the measurement has to be redone at the new bucket width. Also note three places independently encode the yaw count: render.py YAWS, iso.gd's 90 * roundi(deg/90) bucketing, and iso.gd's 45.0 + hysteresis test
items.why: Raising yaw count silently freezes every turret facing

items.title: tools/shot.py cannot take a menu screenshot and its comment used to claim it could. shot.py unconditionally forwards --anchor and --shot, and menu.gd's _boot_from_cli() tests argv.has('--anchor') or argv.has('--shot') BEFORE it looks at --shot-menu, so --extra --shot-menu is silently dropped and the run screenshots the game instead (confirmed: SHOT/FRAME emitted, MENUFRAME never). The gate's 'menu renders' check reaches it by other means, so this is only a hole in the everyday tool. Fix is a shot.py --menu mode that skips forwarding --anchor/--shot, or a menu.gd precedence change. Found while verifying PRC-09.

CAM-08's real acceptance number was never taken: the issue verifies with tools/shot.py --extra --profile 600, and --profile is CAM-06's deliverable which does not exist in scripts/main.gd yet. The bucketing was proved by a standalone microbenchmark (scripts/test/hit_bucket.gd: per-call cost flat at 2.2-2.9us across 150/300/600/900 units, against a linear reference that climbs 9.3 to 58.1us) plus a 910-query differential test with 0 mismatches. That is the right shape but a different instrument from LF-100's in-engine 7.67ms at 900 units. Re-run the issue's stated command once --profile lands and record the real in-frame number against the 1.0ms target.

The 'whole-frame SHA-256 must match' verification pattern used across several camera and FX issues cannot work on any frame containing combat. combat_fx.gd's sparks, debris and arc jaggedness call randf() unseeded BY DESIGN (a chain node's lightning is meant never to repeat), so two runs of byte-identical source produce different frame hashes: measured 23 differing pixels out of 1166400, one small cluster, max channel delta 279. An agent verifying a presentation-only change against a hash will therefore see a false failure and may go looking for a regression that does not exist. Future issues should specify either a pixel-diff against a repeat-run baseline of the SAME source, or a capture-time RNG seed hook. Found while verifying CAM-08.

The PostToolUse hook that parse-checks an edited .gd file (added to .claude/settings.json by PRC-01) has NOT been observed firing. Its logic was verified by feeding it real stdin JSON in Claude Code's documented shape and it behaves correctly both clean and broken, but no hook output appeared on any live Edit or Write during the session that added it -- most likely because settings.json is read once at session start, before the edit landed. Confirm in a fresh session by deliberately breaking a .gd file with Edit and checking the hook speaks up. If it does not fire, the gate's 'gdscript parses' check is the only line of defence and the hook should be removed rather than left as a comfort that does nothing.

pack_atlas.py --check cannot catch a cell-size mismatch, because 'if not write: continue' short-circuits before Image.open, so the per-image size assertion never runs in check mode. Pre-existing, but it matters now that the cell size comes from sprites.json rather than a hardcoded constant: the assertion is the only thing standing between a manifest that says 512 and renders that are 256. Make --check run the assertion.

Before ART-04 raises the atlas cell, probe GL_MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE on this machine under GL Compatibility. pack_atlas.py's COLS=12 makes a 1024px-cell page 12288px wide; the GL spec floor is 2048 and nothing here has measured what Mesa llvmpipe and the owner's Windows GPU actually report. A page that exceeds it does not warn, it fails to upload. Flagged in a pack_atlas.py comment rather than asserted, because it is unmeasured.

tools/session.py's gate() does not forward --tier to the check.py subprocess (it forwards --no-window only). Harmless today because the default is tier 4, which is what a STATE.md regeneration wants — but a 'fast STATE regen' workflow is the obvious next ask and it would silently record a tier-1 result as though it were the full gate. If --tier is ever forwarded, the gate block STATE.md writes must also record which tier produced it.
items.note: Fixed by PRC-20: tools/session.py --tier now forwards to check.py, and check.py's own summary line already carries the tier, so STATE's Gate block cannot silently overclaim. Verified live — a --tier 1 regen wrote 'tier 1 — 15 passed · 0 failed · 15 skipped' into STATE.

items.title: Concurrent Godot captures do not parallelise -- they multiply. Rendering is Mesa llvmpipe software GL and one capture spreads to about 8 of this machine's 16 cores (measured: a single Godot at 788 percent CPU), so three agents capturing at once drives load average to 18.6 and turns a nine-second frame-1800 capture into minutes. Two agents then hit the 120-second command timeout and stopped mid-task waiting on it, which is how this surfaced. Consequences worth fixing: tools/shot.py should take a lease or a lock so captures serialise across agents rather than trampling each other (this is PRC-07's lease mechanism, and it is the strongest argument for it), and any multi-agent plan should treat 'launches Godot' as a scarce resource and schedule at most one or two such workstreams at a time. Measured during the theatre-scale E1 batch.

The pooled combat FX -- bolt, arc, flak, mortar and field in fx_additive.gd's main _draw() -- do not dim under brownout. Only Display.glow is applied to them, not the brownout factor that glow_layer.gd uses. CLAUDE.md is explicit that the whole reason glow is a separate additive pass is that 'brownout visibly dims every emissive element in the game' (decision 007), and the fight itself is the most emissive thing on screen. Pre-existing; surfaced while adding the sustained beam, which DOES carry the factor, so the two passes now disagree with each other. Fix is the same 0.35 multiply the beam and the glow layer already use.
check.py's module docstring says 'no .github/ directory yet' — stale since PRC-08 added .github/workflows/
items.why: tools/check.py is out of this agent's owned scope for PRC-08; docstring fix needs a session that owns that file
